sections.h2: Selling in Dearborn: the Certificate of Occupancy
sections.html:
Dearborn sellers face one step that most Michigan sellers never see: the city requires a Certificate of Occupancy before a house can close. It comes from a city inspection and is issued in the buyer's name, so the timing has to be planned from the day you decide to sell.

Dearborn is a first-ring suburb in Wayne County, about seven miles west of downtown Detroit, with 105,611 residents in the 2025 estimate. Ford's world headquarters and the River Rouge complex sit here, and many owners live close to a Ford job, a hospital or one of the two colleges. Buyers often start their search with commute time, so a short drive to those places helps a listing.

The seller, the listing agent or a legally appointed power of attorney files a residential inspection request with the city's Economic Development Department and pays the fee with it. City staff then call to set the visit, which takes about 45 minutes. An adult aged 18 or older must be home for the whole inspection.

The inspector checks basic safety and property maintenance against the city's minimum housing standards, then issues a written report. Every item on that report counts as a code violation and has to be fixed and re-inspected. The sequence runs like this:

  • Submit the application and payment.
  • Wait for staff to schedule the inspection.
  • Be present for the walk-through and keep the report.
  • Correct each listed item. The clock is twelve months from the first inspection day.
  • Request a re-inspection and pass it.
  • Email the buyer's name to the city sales address and say whether the buyer will live in the house, so the certificate can be prepared.

A report holds for twelve months, so a house that falls out of contract can be relisted without a second full inspection while that window is open.

Dearborn leans toward owners and larger households. Figures cover 2020 to 2024 unless a row names another date.

With nearly three people in the average household, buyers here often want extra bedrooms and a usable basement. Those are worth pointing out in a listing.

Dearborn sends two bills a year, and each carries different taxing bodies. Whichever bill is open at your closing decides what the settlement statement shows.

  • The summer bill is levied July 1 and due September 14. It holds the school tax, the city tax and the county-allocated operating tax. An owner can pay it in three pieces (September 14, November 14, January 14) for a one-time $3 charge.
  • The winter bill is levied December 1 and due February 14. The county's remaining levies and the city's combined sewer overflow debt ride on it, and the whole amount is paid at once.

Before closing, ask the Treasury Division for a written payoff so the closing agent sends the right amount. The cashier counter is at the Dearborn Administrative Center, 16901 Michigan Avenue, open weekdays until half past four. The Assessment Department shares the building and answers value questions at 313-943-2140.

If a bill is unpaid when you list, bring it up with your buyer early. The closing agent can pay it from your proceeds, but only if the payoff figure is on file before the closing date.

sections.h2: State transfer tax and filings after closing
sections.html:
Michigan puts the transfer tax on the seller. On every $500 block of sale value the state takes $3.75 (MCL 207.525), and Wayne County adds its own levy under MCL 207.504, which sets 55 cents per block in counties under two million residents. Ask Wayne County's deed office for the exact county figure before you build a net sheet.

MCL 207.526 carves out some deeds. Dearborn owners most often meet the exemption for a deed between spouses that changes how they hold title, and the one for a land contract whose legal title has not yet passed.

After closing, the buyer notifies the assessor inside 45 days (MCL 211.27a). For the following tax year the taxable value is set at the SEV, and the inflation cap resumes a year later. If you held a principal residence exemption, ask the Dearborn assessor for the form that removes it.

sections.h2: Which selling route fits a house with open inspection items?
sections.html:
A listed sale usually brings the highest price but makes you finish every cited repair before closing. An investor who plans to renovate or rent the house faces the same certificate requirement, and the city asks whether the buyer intends to live there. A private sale lets you and the buyer agree in writing on who pays for corrections, which helps when the inspection list is long.

A long list is the usual reason a Dearborn sale slips. Book the inspection early, settle in writing who handles each correction, and keep the report in your closing file. A cash buyer who accepts the house as it stands can take the repair list off your plate, though the city still wants its inspection and the buyer's name before it issues the certificate.

Start with the inspection request, because everything else waits on the city's calendar. While you wait for the visit, call the Treasury Division for your payoff and ask Wayne County's deed office what the county transfer tax will be. Those two numbers let you work out what you actually keep from a sale.

Once the report arrives, sort the items into cheap fixes you can finish yourself and larger repairs that need a contractor. Keep receipts and the re-inspection result together in one folder. When you have a contract, send the buyer's name to the city sales address and confirm whether the buyer will occupy the house. The closing agent will want the certificate, the tax payoff and the deed ready at the table, and a missing piece is the most common reason a Dearborn closing gets pushed back.

faqs.q: Is a city inspection required before my Dearborn house can close?
faqs.a: Yes. Dearborn will not let a sale close without a Certificate of Occupancy, and the certificate follows a pre-sale inspection. You, your agent or a power of attorney requests the visit, fixes any violations, passes a re-inspection and then emails the buyer's name to city staff.

faqs.q: How long is a Dearborn inspection report valid?
faqs.a: Twelve months, counting from the first inspection. That is also your window to correct every listed violation and pass the re-inspection, so a failed sale does not force a second full inspection if you relist inside it.

faqs.q: When are Dearborn property taxes due?
faqs.a: Summer taxes are due September 14 and winter taxes February 14. The summer bill may be split into payments on September 14, November 14 and January 14. The winter bill has no split option.

faqs.q: Who pays the state transfer tax in a Dearborn sale?
faqs.a: The seller. Michigan makes the grantor liable, at $3.75 for each $500 block of value for the state plus the Wayne County levy. A few deeds are exempt, such as a spouse's deed creating a tenancy by the entireties.

faqs.q: How does a sale change the tax bill?
faqs.a: It usually rises for the buyer. For the following tax year the taxable value is set at the SEV, and the inflation cap resumes a year later. Your own exemption ends once you rescind it with the assessor.
